concept.name: Replicated Logs & Sequencing

relationships.description: Connects Replicated Logs & Sequencing to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Replicated logs establish a single, totally ordered sequence of commands across distributed nodes so every replica applies the exact same state transitions in the exact same order.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use a consensus-backed replicated log (Raft/Paxos/KRaft) with monotonic term-and-index sequencing whenever multiple nodes must agree on state order despite crashes and network partitions.

concept.whyItMatters: In distributed systems, concurrent client requests arrive at different nodes in different orders due to network jitter, retries, and node failures. Without a globally agreed sequence, replicas diverge into inconsistent states (split-brain). Replicated logs—powering etcd, CockroachDB, Kafka KRaft, and ZooKeeper—turn messy concurrency into deterministic state-machine replication.
whenToUse: Distributed metadata, locks, leader election, or configuration stores require strong linearizable consistency across node failures.
Multiple storage replicas must apply mutations in identical order to guarantee identical B-tree, key-value, or ledger states.
Event-driven pipelines need a durable, replayable, strictly ordered commit log per partition (e.g., Kafka, Pulsar).
whenNotToUse: Eventual consistency or commutative updates (CRDTs, counters, append-only metrics) suffice and cross-AZ consensus latency (1–5ms RTT) is unacceptable.
A single primary database with asynchronous read replicas already meets durability and RPO/RTO requirements.
Workload is pure stateless compute or ephemeral caching where losing in-flight state on restart is harmless.
keyPoints: Every log entry carries a monotonic (term, index) pair: the index orders entries within a log, while the term (epoch) detects stale leaders after network partitions.
A leader sequences all incoming writes, appends them to its local Write-Ahead Log (WAL), and replicates them via AppendEntries RPCs to followers.
An entry is committed only after a strict majority quorum (e.g., 3 of 5 nodes) persists it to durable storage (fsync), guaranteeing survival across any minority failure.
State-machine safety requires that if any node applies log entry at index i, no other node can ever apply a different command at index i.
Compaction via periodic snapshots prevents unbounded log growth while allowing slow or newly joined nodes to catch up without replaying terabytes of history.

examples.title: Kubernetes Control Plane Metadata (etcd / Raft)
examples.scenario: A 5-node etcd cluster stores cluster state, pod scheduling leases, and distributed locks across three availability zones.
examples.outcome: Every API Server write is sequenced by the Raft leader with a monotonic `revision` index, replicated to at least 3 of 5 NVMe-backed nodes in ~3ms p99, and survives up to 2 simultaneous node or AZ failures with zero data loss.

examples.title: Kafka KRaft Partition Replication
examples.scenario: A payment ledger topic uses 3 replicas (`acks=all`, `min.insync.replicas=2`) to sequence 40,000 events/sec per partition.
examples.outcome: The partition leader assigns sequential offsets (`0, 1, 2...`) and advances the High Watermark only after followers persist the batch, ensuring consumers never read uncommitted or out-of-order events during broker failover.

tradeOffs.factor: Strong quorum replication vs. Asynchronous replication
tradeOffs.pro: Quorum replication (`W + R > N`) prevents acknowledged data loss during sudden leader crashes.
tradeOffs.con: Every write pays at least one network round-trip to the fastest quorum of followers plus disk `fsync` latency.

tradeOffs.pro: Single-leader logs eliminate write-write conflicts and simplify reasoning about exact global order.
tradeOffs.con: All writes for a shard/partition bottleneck on one leader node until partitioned across multiple Raft groups (Multi-Raft).

tradeOffs.factor: Aggressive fsync batching vs. Per-write fsync
tradeOffs.pro: Group-committing 50–200 log entries per `fsync` boosts throughput by 10x–30x on NVMe SSDs.
tradeOffs.con: Adds 1–5ms of batching delay to individual write latency.

failureModes.name: Split-Brain / Stale Leader Writes
failureModes.description: A partitioned old leader continues serving reads or accepting writes while the rest of the cluster elects a new leader.
failureModes.mitigation: Require quorum heartbeats (ReadIndex / leader leases) for linearizable reads and pass monotonic fencing tokens (term/epoch) to downstream storage.

failureModes.name: Log Divergence on Unclean Failover
failureModes.description: Uncommitted entries on an isolated node conflict with the new leader's committed log at the same index.
failureModes.mitigation: Consensus protocols (Raft's Log Matching Property) force followers to truncate conflicting uncommitted suffixes and overwrite them with the leader's log.

failureModes.name: Disk I/O Stall Triggering Election Storms
failureModes.description: Slow `fsync` or GC pauses prevent the leader from sending heartbeats within `electionTimeout`, causing repeated failovers.
failureModes.mitigation: Isolate WAL on dedicated NVMe drives, tune `heartbeatInterval` (e.g., 100ms) vs. `electionTimeout` (e.g., 1,000ms), and use Pre-Vote to block disruptive elections.

failureModes.name: Snapshot / Catch-Up Storm
failureModes.description: A restarted node falls far behind, forcing the leader to stream multi-gigabyte snapshots that saturate network bandwidth and starve live replication.
failureModes.mitigation: Rate-limit snapshot transfers, compact logs frequently at bounded sizes (e.g., every 100k entries), and serve snapshots from non-leader learners if supported.

commonMistakes: Deploying an even number of consensus nodes (e.g., 2 or 4), which increases cost without improving fault tolerance (4 nodes still tolerate only 1 failure, same as 3).
Serving stale reads directly from a leader or follower without a ReadIndex check or valid lease, breaking linearizability.
Running WAL and heavy compaction/application workloads on the same shared disk, causing tail-latency spikes and spurious leader elections.
Disabling `fsync` on the consensus log—if a power loss wipes an acknowledged entry on a quorum, committed state is permanently corrupted.
Assuming a single Raft group can scale indefinitely instead of sharding into Multi-Raft ranges (as CockroachDB and TiKV do).

sections.content:
## The idea

State Machine Replication (SMR) rests on a simple theorem: if two deterministic state machines start in the same initial state and execute the **exact same sequence of inputs**, they will arrive at the exact same final state.

A **replicated log** is the mechanism that manufactures that identical sequence across unreliable machines. Instead of replicating complex in-memory structures, a designated **leader** assigns each command a strictly increasing `(term, index)` coordinate, appends it to an append-only Write-Ahead Log (WAL), and replicates it to followers. Once a **majority quorum** (`floor(N/2) + 1`) persists the entry, it becomes **committed** and is safely applied to the local state machine.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `PUT /accounts/42 balance=500` write on a **3-node Raft cluster** (`N1` Leader, `N2` and `N3` Followers) in `term=7`:

1. **Sequence & local append**: `N1` receives the client request, assigns `index=1042, term=7`, and writes the entry to its local NVMe WAL (`fsync`).
2. **Parallel replication**: `N1` sends `AppendEntries(term=7, prevLogIndex=1041, prevLogTerm=7, entries=[1042], leaderCommit=1041)` to `N2` and `N3`.
3. **Consistency check & persist**: `N2` verifies its log has `(term=7, index=1041)`, appends `1042`, calls `fsync`, and replies `success=true`. (`N3` may be temporarily slow or partitioned.)
4. **Quorum commit**: `N1` now has 2 of 3 confirmations (`N1` + `N2`), forming a majority. `N1` advances `commitIndex = 1042`, applies `PUT /accounts/42` to its local KV engine, and returns `200 OK` to the client.
5. **Follower apply**: On the next heartbeat (within 100ms), `N1` advertises `leaderCommit=1042`; `N2` and (once caught up) `N3` apply index `1042` to their state machines.

sections.content:
## The invariants that prevent divergence

Correct log sequencing depends on three non-negotiable invariants:

- **Election Restriction**: A candidate cannot win an election unless its log is at least as up-to-date (higher last term, or equal term and >= last index) as a majority of nodes. This guarantees the new leader already holds every previously committed entry.
- **Log Matching Property**: If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, they are guaranteed identical for all preceding entries—enforced by checking `(prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm)` on every `AppendEntries`.
- **Current-Term Commit Rule**: A leader never marks entries from an *older* term as committed by counting replicas alone; it commits them indirectly by committing a new entry from its *current* term.

## Replicated log implementations compared

| System | Protocol | Fault Tolerance (N=3 / N=5) | Typical Write Latency | Primary Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **etcd** | Raft | 1 / 2 nodes | 2–5 ms (NVMe) | Kubernetes metadata, service discovery, locks |
| **Kafka KRaft** | Raft-variant | 1 / 2 brokers (ISR) | 2–10 ms (batched) | High-throughput partitioned event streaming |
| **CockroachDB** | Multi-Raft | 1 / 2 per range | 3–15 ms (geo-dependent) | Horizontally sharded distributed SQL |
| **ZooKeeper** | Zab | 1 / 2 nodes | 2–6 ms | Legacy coordination, leader election, config |

## Failure modes and split-brain prevention

The subtlest bugs in replicated logs happen during **asymmetric partitions** and **clock drift**:

- **Zombie leader reads**: If `N1` is partitioned, `N2` wins `term=8`, but `N1` doesn't know yet and serves stale reads from memory. Fix: use **ReadIndex** (leader confirms quorum heartbeat before replying) or bounded hardware-clock leases.
- **Fencing downstream side effects**: If a leader writes to external S3/DB storage after losing leadership, pass the Raft `term` or ZooKeeper `zxid` as a **fencing token** so storage rejects stale epochs.
- **Unbounded WAL growth**: Without log compaction into snapshots, restart recovery time grows linearly with cluster lifetime.

## Throughput and tail-latency tuning

To hit tens of thousands of consensus writes per second without sacrificing safety, production engines use **pipelining** (sending batch `N+1` before `N` is acked), **group commit** (coalescing concurrent client writes into one `fsync`), **witness/learner nodes** (voting-free replicas for analytics), and **Multi-Raft sharding** so independent key ranges elect leaders across all nodes.

## Practical checklist

- **Deploy odd cluster sizes (3 or 5)**: Use 3 nodes for single-failure tolerance and 5 nodes if you need maintenance + 1 unexpected failure.
- **Use dedicated NVMe for WAL**: Keep log `fsync` p99 below 2–3 ms by isolating WAL from application/compaction I/O.
- **Enable Pre-Vote**: Prevent partitioned nodes from incrementing terms and disrupting healthy leaders upon reconnect.
- **Configure automated snapshots**: Compact logs at fixed byte thresholds (e.g., 64–256 MB) to bound recovery time.
- **Monitor leader-change rate**: Alert on >1 leader election per hour—frequent elections indicate network drops or disk stalls.

interviewProblems.title: Replicated Logs & Sequencing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Replicated Logs & Sequencing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Replicated logs establish a single, totally ordered sequence of commands across distributed nodes so every replica applies the exact same state transitions in the exact same order.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Follower Quorum applies the primary invariant and coordinates with State Machine.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, State Machine experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Require quorum heartbeats (ReadIndex / leader leases) for linearizable reads and pass monotonic fencing tokens (term/epoch) to downstream storage.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use a consensus-backed replicated log (Raft/Paxos/KRaft) with monotonic term-and-index sequencing whenever multiple nodes must agree on state order despite crashes and network partitions.
Avoid trap: Deploying an even number of consensus nodes (e.g., 2 or 4), which increases cost without improving fault tolerance (4 nodes still tolerate only 1 failure, same as 3).
Avoid trap: Serving stale reads directly from a leader or follower without a ReadIndex check or valid lease, breaking linearizability.
When to reach for it: Distributed metadata, locks, leader election, or configuration stores require strong linearizable consistency across node failures.
When to reach for it: Multiple storage replicas must apply mutations in identical order to guarantee identical B-tree, key-value, or ledger states.

putItTogether.title: Putting Replicated Logs Sequencing Together
putItTogether.summary: Use a consensus-backed replicated log (Raft/Paxos/KRaft) with monotonic term-and-index sequencing whenever multiple nodes must agree on state order despite crashes and network partitions.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Replicated Logs Sequencing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Every API Server write is sequenced by the Raft leader with a monotonic `revision` index, replicated to at least 3 of 5 NVMe-backed nodes in ~3ms p99, and survives up to 2 simultaneous node or AZ failures with zero data loss.
